sections.title: Grammar
sections.html:
Read across. A reads the question. B says the answer.

Grammar Box 1: been + -ing (the activity, still going on)

QUESTIONANSWER
How long have you been working here?I've been working here for two years.
How long have you been working at the hotel?I've been working there for two years.
How long has she been taking this class?She's been taking this class since September.

Grammar Box 2: have + past participle is also correct for How long

QUESTIONANSWER
How long have you worked here?I've worked here since 2024.
How long have you worked there?I've worked there for two years.
Have you finished the training?Yes, I have.

Grammar Box 3: a finished time needs the simple past

QUESTIONANSWER
What did you do in your last job?I helped customers at a store.
Where did you work in 2022?I worked at a bakery in 2022.

Grammar Box 4: Which form?

FORMEXAMPLE
been + -ingthe activity, still going on: I've been working here for two years.
have + past participlealso correct for How long: I've worked here since 2024.
simple pasta finished time (in 2022): I worked at a bakery in 2022.

Rule of thumb: been + -ing stresses the activity, still going on. have + past participle is also correct for How long, and it is the form from Level 4. Both answers are accepted. A finished time (in 2022) still needs the simple past.

Questions and answers

Q: Can I say I am working here since 2024?

A: No. Say I've been working here since 2024. I've worked here since 2024 is also correct.

Q: Can I say I've been working here in 2022?

A: No. That year is finished. Say I worked here in 2022.

Q: Is I've worked there for two years wrong?

A: No. For How long, both been working and worked are accepted when you still have the job.

Practice A: Write the missing word.

  1. I've been ____________ here for two years.
  2. I've worked here ____________ 2024.
  3. I've worked here ____________ two years.
  4. I ____________ at a bakery in 2022.
  5. Have you ____________ the training?
  6. She's been ____________ this class since September.

Practice B: Circle the correct words.

  1. I (am working / 've been working) here since 2024.
  2. I ('ve been working / worked) here in 2022.
  3. How long (have you been working / you have been working) at the hotel?
  4. I've (been working / working) there for two years.
  5. I've worked there (for / since) two years.
  6. She's been taking this class (since / for) September.

Common mistakes

✗ Don't say✓ Say
I am working here since 2024.I've been working here since 2024. or I've worked here since 2024.
I've been working here in 2022.I worked here in 2022.

Pair check

A says still true or finished in 2022. B makes one sentence (I've been working… or I worked…). Then switch.

sections.title: Read & Write
sections.html:
A. Read. Read once for the job. Then find the answers.

Harbor Hotel · Front Desk Clerk · How we interview

The Harbor Hotel is hiring a front-desk clerk. This page is practice for class. It is not a real job offer. Bring a résumé if you have one. A name tag helps, but you can also say your name. You do not need every qualification tonight.

We want someone who has been working with customers for one year or more. You may also say, "I have worked with customers for one year." Both answers are fine when the work is still true. A finished job needs the simple past and the year. One example in the posting is, "I worked at a bakery in 2022."

Please bring one accomplishment and one example. An accomplishment is one thing you did well. In the posting, the accomplishment is "I trained two new cashiers." The example is "I stayed with one new cashier for a week." A skill is smaller. Greeting a guest is a skill. You can name one skill in a single line.

How we interview: First we ask, "How long have you been working with customers?" Next we ask for the accomplishment and the example. Then you ask one follow-up question. A handshake at the start is welcome. After the practice, the coach sends a short follow-up note. You can keep that note in your portfolio.

Front-desk training starts next month. You do not have to finish the training before this practice. Tell us one skill you use now. We do not ask why you left a job, what you earn, or how you came to this city. You may invent the hotel and the dates. Four clear sentences are enough.

B. Answer the questions.

  1. What job is the posting for? ______________________________________________
  2. How long with customers? ______________________________________________
  3. What example do they give? ______________________________________________
  4. A finished job in 2022 uses… ______________________________________________
  5. What does the coach send after? ______________________________________________

C. Write a 6–8 sentence email to the coach. Name the job you want to practice, how long you have been doing related work, and one accomplishment with an example. Invented details are fine.

Example: I want to practice for a front-desk job. I've been working with customers for three years. I've worked at a store since 2023. One accomplishment is that I trained two new cashiers. For example, I stayed with one cashier for a week. I worked at a bakery in 2022. That job is finished. I want to ask one follow-up question at the end.

My email

lessons.teacher:
How to Use This Plan

Teach in English. You do not need to speak the learners' languages. Show the picture, draw the line, and point to the grammar box. There is no contrast-tip box. The common mix-up is a row in the mistakes table.

Instructions: use the same short task words: Listen. Circle. Check. Write. Work with a partner. Ask a follow-up question. Give a reason.

Instruction rule: Model it (do it with one learner while everyone watches), check it (ask: "Is the job still true, or is the year finished?"), then go.

When a learner is stuck: (1) show it (picture, gesture, or the timeline); (2) give one more English example; (3) point to the grammar box; (4) a classmate can help for a few seconds, then back to English.

About four sentences: the Talk Time answer and the exit ticket are about four connected sentences: how long, what you have been doing, one example, and why it matters.

Lesson 1 (Week 1): How Long Have You Been Working Here?

At a glance

Objectives: learners can…

  • answer How long have you been…?
  • also answer with I've worked… for / since
  • give one example of an accomplishment
  • ask a follow-up question

Materials

  • Student Pages for Lesson 1 (print the number you expect + 3 spares)
  • Board and markers. Draw a line: 2022 (finished) ————→ now (still true)
  • Six interview question cards (they are on the Talk Time page; cut them if you can)
  • Listening: L5_L1_listening.mp3 (1:37). Play it two times. No speaker? Read the script aloud with a volunteer.
  • Prep time: 15 minutes. Read the plan, draw the line, and practice the script once.

Key vocabulary (with pictures on the New Words page)

★ résumé • ★ interview • ★ accomplishment • ★ example • ★ skill • ★ job offer • ★ training • ★ portfolio • ★ handshake • ★ follow-up • qualification • name tag

Clock-time plan

Times are loose. If listening or Talk Time runs long, take the time from Read & Write.

5 or fewer: one table. For Talk Time, each person interviews the person on their left.

Step by step

Step 1 · 6:00–6:06 · Opening Talk · 6 min

  • Grouping: pairs. 15 learners: 7 pairs + 1 group of 3. 7–8 learners: 3–4 pairs. 5 or fewer: pairs, or one group with you.
  • Week 1: there is no homework to check. Say: "Welcome. Tonight is practice, not a real interview. You may invent the hotel and the dates."
  • Before class: write on the board: How long have you…? and I've been…
  • Opening Talk: learners open the Opening Talk page. A asks a card question. B answers in a short summary (the answer, one detail). A asks one follow-up. Then switch.
  • Model with one learner: "How long have you lived in this city?" Help the learner answer in two or three sentences. Then ask, "How long? Can you give an example?"
  • Late arrivals: join any pair.
  • If behind: one card only.

Step 2 · 6:06–6:12 · New Words · 6 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs.
  • Do: point to each picture and say the word. Learners repeat once. ★ = most important.
  • Show the hard words: a résumé is a paper about your work. An accomplishment is one thing you did well. An example makes it easy to see. A follow-up comes after the interview (a note or a call). A qualification is a fact that shows you can do the job. A name tag shows your name. It is not a skill.
  • Check the meaning: "Is a résumé a paper about your work?" (yes, a work paper) • "Is a handshake a follow-up?" (no) • "Does a name tag show a skill?" (no, it shows a name)
  • Partner game (about 2 min): A points to a picture and asks one question. B answers. Switch. 15 learners: finish with 3 teams if you have a minute. 7–8: 2 teams. 5 or fewer: one team against the clock.
  • If behind: teach the ★ words only.

Step 3 · 6:12–6:32 · Listening + "Hear it, say it" · 20 min

  • Grouping: individuals, then pairs. With 5 or fewer, check together.
  • Before you listen: "Nora is practicing for a hotel front-desk job. Samir is her coach. Ms. Hale asks the questions. Listen: what job is the practice for?"
  • Voices: Nora, Samir, and Ms. Hale. A narrator opens and closes. The audio is recorded (about 1:37). Read the script with volunteers, two times. Press nothing. A third read is fine if the class needs it.
  • Play 1 → Task A (the main idea). Pairs compare. Check together: b. a hotel front-desk job.
  • Read Tasks B and C so learners know what to listen for.
  • Play 2 → Tasks B and C. Pairs compare. Then show the answers.
  • "Hear it, say it": gonna and wanna are short forms. This listening uses the full forms. You can say going to and want to. Then the weak been in I've been working. Stress the job word, not been. Say each line two times.
  • If behind: do Task C together on the board.

Step 4 · 6:32–6:45 · Grammar Q&A · 13 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. The left side is the question. The right side is the answer.
  • Draw the timeline (1 min): two marks. Left: 2022, finished: I worked at a bakery. Right: now, still true: I've been working / I've worked. Say: "been + -ing stresses the activity, still going on. have + past participle is also correct for How long. Both answers are accepted. A finished time (in 2022) still needs the simple past."
  • Boxes: read across. Box 1 is been + -ing. Box 2 is have + past participle, also correct. Box 3 is the simple past for a finished job. Box 4 is which form.
  • Rule of thumb: been + -ing stresses the activity, still going on. have + past participle is also correct for How long, and it is the form from Level 4. Both answers are accepted. A finished time (in 2022) still needs the simple past.
  • Questions and answers: read each question. The class says the right sentence.
  • Practice A and B: learners write, then pairs check.
  • Common mistakes: read "Don't say" and ask for the fix before you show "Say."
  • Pair check (last 2 min): A says "still true" or "finished in 2022." B makes one sentence. Switch.
  • If behind: skip the pair check. Talk Time practices it.

Break · 6:45–7:00 · 15 min

  • Leave the timeline on the board: still true → I've been working / I've worked. A finished year → I worked.

Step 5 · 7:00–7:18 · Talk Time: Practice Interview + Kind Feedback · 18 min

  • Model a 30-second answer first: "I've been working with customers for three years. One accomplishment is that I trained two new cashiers. For example, I stayed with one cashier for a week. It matters because new workers need a calm start."
  • Round 1, Practice Interview: A is the interviewer and uses the six question cards. B answers in about four sentences (how long, one accomplishment, one example, one reason). Then switch.
  • Round 2, Kind Feedback: the partner names one clear sentence and asks one follow-up.
  • 15 learners: pairs, then one rotation.
  • 7–8 learners: pairs. You listen to each pair for the baseline. Prompts, if you need them: How long have you been coming to this class? Tell me about a project you finished. What do you wish you had asked someone? Do you know if the library is open tonight? Tell me one thing a person said to you this week. About five learners tonight. The same prompts come back at the final. Do not ask why someone left a job, what they earn, or how they came to this country.
  • 5 or fewer: one table. Each person interviews the person on their left.
  • If behind: round 1 only.

Step 6 · 7:18–7:25 · Read & Write · 7 min

  • Grouping: pairs read; then each person starts the email. With 5 or fewer, read the posting aloud together.
  • Read: the Harbor Hotel posting and the "How we interview" note. Say: "Read once for the job. Then find the answers."
  • Questions: pairs answer. Then show the key.
  • Write: a 6–8 sentence email to the coach. Name the job you want to practice, how long you have been doing related work, and one accomplishment with an example. Invented details are fine. Start in class. Finish at home.
  • If behind: the questions only. The email is homework.

Step 7 · 7:25–7:30 · Can-do check + Exit Ticket + Homework · 5 min · NEVER SKIP

  • Can-do check (about 1 min): read the four "I can" lines. Learners mark one face for each line: 😀 🙂 😐. Every goal is a good goal. This is the Week 1 check, not a test.
  • Exit ticket: How long have you been studying English (or doing your job)? About four sentences: how long, what you have been doing, one example, and why it matters. With 5 or fewer, a learner can say it and then write it.
  • Collect the pages. Sort them later into yes / almost / not yet. Next class, put two corrections on the board. No names.
  • Homework: about 20–25 minutes. Do item 1 together: I / work / at the hotel / for two years (still true) → I've been working at the hotel for two years. (I've worked at the hotel for two years is also correct.)

Listening script

Audio is recorded (about 1:37). Read it with volunteers at a natural, friendly speed. The spoken lines use going to and want to. gonna and wanna are short forms. This listening uses the full forms.

Narrator: Lesson one. The community center is holding a practice interview night. Nora wants a hotel front-desk job.

Samir: Hi, Nora. I'm Samir, your coach. Are you ready to practice?

Nora: Yes. I want to practice for a front-desk job at the Harbor Hotel.

Samir: Good. Ms. Hale is going to ask the questions. I am going to take notes.

Ms. Hale: Welcome, Nora. How long have you been working with customers?

Nora: I've been working with customers for three years. I work at a store now.

Ms. Hale: Tell me one accomplishment.

Nora: I trained two new cashiers last spring.

Ms. Hale: Can you give an example?

Nora: Yes. One new cashier was nervous. I stayed with her for a week.

Ms. Hale: Have you finished any hotel training?

Nora: Not yet. I want to start the front-desk training next month.

Samir: That example was clear. You said, "I've been working."

Ms. Hale: What did you do in 2022?

Nora: I worked at a bakery in 2022. That job is finished.

Ms. Hale: Do you have a follow-up question?

Nora: Yes. What do you send after the interview?

Ms. Hale: A short note. A handshake and a thank-you are a good start.

Samir: Next, you are going to put one accomplishment in your portfolio.

Narrator: That's the end of the listening.

Answer key

  • Check the meaning: 1 yes, a work paper. 2 no. 3 no, it shows a name.
  • Listening Task A: b. a hotel front-desk job.
  • Listening Task B: 1 three years. 2 trained two new cashiers. 3 stayed for a week. 4 a bakery.
  • Listening Task C: 1 been working. 2 worked. 3 been working. 4 worked.
  • Grammar Practice A: 1 working. 2 since. 3 for. 4 worked. 5 finished. 6 taking.
  • Grammar Practice B: 1 've been working. 2 worked. 3 have you been working. 4 been working. 5 for. 6 since.
  • Talk Time: answers will vary. A good answer has how long, one accomplishment, one example, and one reason.
  • Homework 1: 1 She's been taking this class since September. 2 I worked at a bakery in 2022. 3 They've been working here since 2024. (They've worked here since 2024 is also correct.) 4 He helped customers at a store. Homework 2 and 3: answers will vary. Homework 4: 1 for. 2 since. 3 for. 4 since.
  • Read & Write: 1 Front desk at Harbor Hotel. 2 For one year or more. 3 Stayed for a week. 4 The simple past. 5 A short follow-up note.
  • Exit ticket: answers will vary. A good answer: "I've been studying English for two years. I've been taking this class since September. One example is my interview practice tonight. It matters because I want to give a clear answer."

Teacher notes

  • This is practice. Do not ask why someone left a job, what they earn, or how they came to this country. Learners may invent the hotel and the dates. Model a 30-second answer first.
  • Both forms are accepted when the work is still true: I've been working here since 2024 and I've worked here since 2024. Do not mark the Level 4 form wrong.
  • A finished year (in 2022) needs the simple past. I've been working here in 2022 is the mix-up to fix.
  • Baseline: during Talk Time, listen to about five learners. Use the prompts in Step 5. Write a few words for your folder. It is not a grade you announce.
  • Reductions: the script says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna. Learners only need to recognize the short forms. They can always say the full forms.
  • Weak been: in I've been working, been sounds like "bin." Stress the job word (working, customers), not been.

Priya and Ben work at a new bakery. Ms. Cole, the inspector, visits before opening day.

A. Listen. Is the bakery open yet? Circle.

a. Yes. It is open now. b. No. It opens tomorrow. c. No. It failed the visit.

B. Listen again. What happened first, second, third, fourth, and last? Circle.

  1. First: (cleaned the kitchen / the poster / the inspector)
  2. Second: (the oven arrived / opening day / the ribbon)
  3. Third: (we painted / we opened / we failed)
  4. Fourth: (the poster went up / the oven / the permit)
  5. Last: (the inspector / the oven / the sign)

C. Listen again. Write had or the simple past.

  1. We ____________ already painted the walls.
  2. You ____________ last.
  3. Ben ____________ already cleaned the kitchen.
  4. The poster ____________ up.
  5. We ____________ already picked up the permit.
  6. The oven ____________ delivered.

Hear it, say it

gonna and wanna are short forms. This listening uses the full forms. You can say going to and want to.

Say the full word had. had and have are different. Say each line two times.

  1. We want to open tomorrow.
  2. We are going to cut the ribbon.
  3. We had already painted the walls.
  4. By the time the inspector arrived, we had painted.

sections.title: Grammar
sections.html:
Read across. A reads the question. B says the answer.

Grammar Box 1: by the time and when

QUESTIONANSWER
What had you done by the time the inspector arrived?We had already painted the walls.
What had Ben done when the oven was delivered?Ben had already cleaned the kitchen.
Had you finished the sign before the poster went up?Yes, we had. / No, we hadn't.

Grammar Box 2: earlier and later

EARLIER: had + past participleLATER: simple past
we had already painted the wallsthe inspector arrived
Ben had already cleaned the kitchenthe oven was delivered
we had finished the signthe poster went up

Grammar Box 3: the later moment's background

QUESTIONANSWER
What was the painter doing when the inspector knocked?The painter was still working.

Grammar Box 4: Which time?

FORMEXAMPLE
earlier pasthad + past participle: we had already painted
later pastsimple past: the inspector arrived
by the timemarks the later time: By the time the inspector arrived, …

Rule of thumb: the earlier past uses had + past participle. The later past uses the simple past. By the time marks the later time.

Questions and answers

Q: Where does already go?

A: Before had's participle: we had already painted. Not we already painted for the earlier time.

Q: Which half of by the time is later?

A: The by the time half. By the time the inspector arrived is later. we had painted is earlier.

Q: Yes, we did or Yes, we had?

A: After Had you…?, say Yes, we had.

Practice A: Write had or the simple past.

  1. By the time the inspector arrived, we ____________ already painted the walls.
  2. When the oven was delivered, Ben ____________ already cleaned the kitchen.
  3. The inspector ____________ after the painting.
  4. The poster ____________ up after the sign.
  5. Had you finished the sign? Yes, we ____________.
  6. The painter ____________ still working when the inspector knocked.

Practice B: Circle the correct words.

  1. By the time the inspector (arrived / had arrived), we had already painted.
  2. We (already painted / had already painted) the walls.
  3. By the time we (had opened / opened), the inspector had arrived.
  4. When the oven (was delivered / had delivered), Ben had cleaned the kitchen.
  5. Had you finished the sign? (Yes, we had. / Yes, we did.)
  6. The painter (was working / had worked) when the inspector knocked.

Common mistakes

✗ Don't say✓ Say
When the inspector arrived, we already painted.When the inspector arrived, we had already painted.
By the time we had opened, the inspector arrived.By the time we opened, the inspector had arrived.

sections.title: Read & Write
sections.html:
A. Read Priya's note to the staff.

Project update · Opening day is tomorrow

Opening day is tomorrow. The bakery is not open yet. This note is the order of the work, so the next shift can see what was already done.

By the time Ms. Cole arrived, we had already painted the walls. When the oven was delivered, Ben had already cleaned the kitchen. We had already picked up the permit before we painted. Had we finished the store sign before the poster went up? Yes, we had. The sign went up first. The poster went up after the sign, and it was already up when the inspector arrived.

The painter was still working when Ms. Cole knocked. He stopped. The walls are dry now. She looked at the permit, the oven, and the clean kitchen. She said we can open tomorrow. She needed the permit and dry paint before she could say yes.

Here is the same order in one list. First, Ben cleaned the kitchen. Second, the oven arrived. Third, we painted the walls. Fourth, the poster went up. Last, the inspector arrived. The ribbon is still on the counter. We are going to hang it in the morning. We want every guest to see it on the door. The display case was ready before her visit, and the awning was already up. The paint roller is in the back room. Please do not leave it on the counter.

If you write about your own project, use by the time once and had already once. A class, a team at work, or a move inside the city is enough. You may invent the details. Please do not describe a move between countries. This note is practice. It is not a real city permit.

B. Answer the questions.

  1. Is the bakery open yet? ______________________________________________
  2. What had Ben done when the oven was delivered? ______________________________________________
  3. What had they done by the time Ms. Cole arrived? ______________________________________________
  4. Which went up first? ______________________________________________
  5. What did she need before she said yes? ______________________________________________

C. Write a 6–8 sentence note about a project you finished. Use by the time once and had already once. Invented details are fine. (Writing check 1.)

Example: By the time the class show started, we had already set the chairs. When the teacher arrived, I had already printed the sign. The order mattered because guests needed a place to sit. We had already checked the list before the door opened.

How to Use This Plan

Teach in English. You do not need to speak the learners' languages. Draw two X's on a line. There is no contrast-tip box. The common mix-up is a row in the mistakes table.

Instructions: Listen. Circle. Number. Write. Work with a partner. Give a reason.

Instruction rule: Model it, check it ("Which time is earlier?"), then go.

When a learner is stuck: show the two X's, give one more English example, point to the grammar box, let a classmate help for a few seconds, then stay in English.

About four sentences: the exit ticket is four sentences: an earlier event, a later event, one more event, and why the order mattered.

Lesson 2 (Week 2): By the Time We Opened

At a glance

Objectives: learners can…

  • say what had already happened
  • use by the time and when with two past times
  • put four events in order
  • write a short project note

Materials

  • Student Pages for Lesson 2 (print the number you expect + 3 spares)
  • Board and markers. Two X's: left = earlier: had painted; right = later: the inspector arrived
  • Four picture cards from the bakery set, one pack per pair (bakery, oven, paint roller, inspector). Shuffle them.
  • Listening: L5_L2_listening.mp3 (1:39). Play it two times. No speaker? Read the script aloud with a volunteer.
  • Prep time: 15 minutes. Draw the line. Shuffle the card packs.

Key vocabulary (with pictures on the New Words page)

★ bakery • ★ oven • ★ permit • ★ inspector • ★ paint roller • ★ store sign • ★ ribbon • ★ opening day • ★ counter • ★ display case • awning • poster

Clock-time plan

Step by step

Step 1 · 6:00–6:06 · Opening Talk + Homework Check · 6 min

  • Grouping: pairs. 15 learners: 7 pairs + 1 group of 3. 7–8: 3–4 pairs. 5 or fewer: pairs, or one group with you.
  • Opening: one question from last week. A asks. B answers in a short summary. A asks one follow-up. Then switch.
  • Model: "How long have you been studying English?" If the learner says I am studying since September, point to the Lesson 1 fix: I've been studying since September or I've studied since September.
  • Homework check (last 2 min): pairs read one sentence from Lesson 1 Homework item 1. You write two corrections on the board. No names.
  • If behind: one card only.

Step 2 · 6:06–6:12 · New Words · 6 min

  • Do: point, say, repeat. ★ = most important.
  • Show the hard words: the oven bakes. It is not a person. The inspector visits before opening day. A permit is the paper that says the work is allowed. A paint roller spreads paint on a wall. The awning is a cover over the door, not a cake. The store sign and the poster are two different things. In our story, the sign went up first.
  • Check the meaning: "Is the oven a person?" (no, it bakes) • "Who comes before opening day?" (the inspector) • "Is an awning a cover or a cake?" (a cover)
  • Partner game: A points to two pictures and asks, "Which one comes first in a bakery opening?" B answers with before. Switch.
  • If behind: the ★ words only.

Step 3 · 6:12–6:32 · Listening + "Hear it, say it" · 20 min

  • Before you listen: "Priya and Ben work at a new bakery. Ms. Cole, the inspector, visits before opening day. Listen: is the bakery open yet?"
  • Voices: Priya, Ben, and Ms. Cole. A narrator opens and closes. Audio is recorded (about 1:39). Read the script two times.
  • Play 1 → Task A. Answer: b. No. It opens tomorrow.
  • Play 2 → Tasks B and C. B is the order of five events. C is had or the simple past.

  • If behind: Task C on the board.

Step 4 · 6:32–6:45 · Grammar Q&A · 13 min

  • Draw two X's. Label the left one "earlier: had painted" and the right one "later: the inspector arrived."
  • Rule of thumb: the earlier past uses had + past participle. The later past uses the simple past. By the time marks the later time.
  • Read the boxes across. Box 1 is by the time and when. Box 2 is earlier and later. Box 3 is the past continuous at the later moment. Box 4 is the rule in three lines.
  • Questions and answers: Had you finished the sign before the poster went up? → Yes, we had. / No, we hadn't.
  • Practice, mistakes, then the pair check: A says a later time (the inspector arrived). B says what had already happened. Switch.
  • If behind: skip the pair check.

Break · 6:45–7:00 · 15 min

  • Leave the two X's on the board.

Step 5 · 7:00–7:18 · Talk Time · 18 min

  • 7–8 learners: pairs, then one switch. Listen to the learners who did not do the baseline last week.

  • Write a 6–8 sentence note about a project you finished (a class, a move inside the city, a team at work). Use by the time once and had already once. Invented details are fine. This is writing check 1. Start in class. Finish at home. You will write one strength and one fix. Learners keep the note in a folder.
  • If behind: questions only.

Step 7 · 7:25–7:30 · Exit Ticket + Homework · 5 min · NEVER SKIP

  • Exit ticket: Tell one change, in order. Four sentences with by the time or had already, plus a reason the order mattered.
  • Collect and sort into yes / almost / not yet. Next week, two corrections, no names.
  • Homework: about 20–25 minutes. Do item 1 together: By the time the inspector arrived, we had already painted the walls.

Listening script

Audio is recorded (about 1:39). Read it with volunteers at a natural, friendly speed. The spoken lines use going to and want to. gonna and wanna are short forms. This listening uses the full forms.

Narrator: Lesson two. Priya and Ben work at a new bakery. Opening day is tomorrow. Ms. Cole, the inspector, is here today.

Ms. Cole: Good morning. I'm Ms. Cole. Is the bakery open yet?

Priya: Not yet. We want to open tomorrow. We are going to cut the ribbon in the morning.

Ms. Cole: What had you already finished before I arrived?

Ben: By the time you arrived, we had already painted the walls.

Priya: When the oven was delivered, Ben had already cleaned the kitchen.

Ms. Cole: Had you finished the store sign before the poster went up?

Ben: Yes, we had. The sign was first. Then the poster went up.

Priya: We had already picked up the permit before we painted.

Ben: First I cleaned the kitchen. Second, the oven arrived. Third, we painted. Fourth, the poster went up. You arrived last.

Ms. Cole: Was the painter still working when I knocked?

Priya: Yes. The painter was still working. The walls are dry now.

Ms. Cole: The display case and the awning look ready. You can open tomorrow.

Ben: The counter was ready yesterday. Thank you.

Ms. Cole: Bring the permit to the door in the morning.

Ben: We will. It is already in the folder.

Priya: We want to tell the staff tonight. We are going to hang the ribbon in the morning.

Narrator: That's the end of the listening.

Answer key

  • Check the meaning: 1 no, it bakes. 2 the inspector. 3 a cover.
  • Listening Task A: b. No. It opens tomorrow.
  • Listening Task B: 1 cleaned the kitchen. 2 the oven arrived. 3 we painted. 4 the poster went up. 5 the inspector.
  • Listening Task C: 1 had. 2 arrived. 3 had. 4 went. 5 had. 6 was.
  • Grammar Practice A: 1 had. 2 had. 3 arrived. 4 went. 5 had. 6 was.
  • Grammar Practice B: 1 arrived. 2 had already painted. 3 opened. 4 was delivered. 5 Yes, we had. 6 was working.
  • Talk Time: answers will vary. Four events, in order, with had already or by the time.
  • Homework 1: 1 By the time the inspector arrived, we had already painted the walls. 2 When the oven was delivered, Ben had already cleaned the kitchen. 3 Yes, we had. 4 The painter was still working when the inspector knocked. Homework 2 and 3: answers will vary. Homework 4: 1 I've been working. 2 worked. 3 I've worked. 4 She's been taking.
  • Read & Write: 1 No. It opens tomorrow. 2 He had cleaned the kitchen. 3 They had painted the walls. 4 The store sign was first. 5 The permit and dry paint.
  • Exit ticket: answers will vary. A good answer: "By the time the inspector arrived, we had already painted the walls. When the oven was delivered, Ben had already cleaned the kitchen. The poster went up after the sign. The order mattered because the inspector needed the permit and dry paint."

Teacher notes

  • Draw two X's and leave them up all night. Left: "earlier: had painted." Right: "later: the inspector arrived."
  • Say the full had. We'd already is easy to miss, and have is a different time. This lesson keeps had strong.
  • The by the time half is the later event. By the time we had opened, the inspector arrived swaps the times. The fix is By the time we opened, the inspector had arrived.
  • Projects can be invented. Do not ask learners to describe a move between countries. A class, a team at work, or a move inside the city is enough.
  • Writing check 1: the 6–8 sentence note. Write one strength and one fix. Learners keep it.
  • Reductions: the script says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna. Learners only need to recognize the short forms.

sections.html:
Read across. A reads the question. B says the answer.

Grammar Box 1: a wish about now

WISHMEANING
I wish I knew the deadline.a wish about now
I wish I had a reminder.had means owned
I wish I were on the list.were, for now

Grammar Box 2: a wish about the past

WISHMEANING
I wish I had asked the tutor.a past regret
I wish I had set an alarm.had + participle
I wish we had signed up on Monday.the sign-up is finished

Grammar Box 3: one different past

IFRESULT
If I had asked, I would have known.one pattern
If he had set an alarm, he would have arrived on time.same pattern
If we had read the reminder, we would have signed up.same pattern

Grammar Box 4: should have, and next time

NOWNEXT
I should have asked earlier.same idea as the wish
Next time I will ask on the first day.a plan
If I had another chance, I would ask.next time

Rule of thumb: A wish about now uses a past verb (knew, had, were). A wish about the past uses had + participle. After If I had + participle, the other half is would have + participle.

A. Read. Read once. Then find the answers.

A note from the tutor

You missed the workshop sign-up. This note is from the class tutor. It is practice for class. It is not a grade. It is not about your family, your money, or a job. The problem is small. The sign-up date passed before you wrote your name on the sheet.

Start with a wish about now. You can say, "I wish I knew the deadline." Knew is a past form, and it talks about right now. You do not know the deadline today. You can also say, "I wish I had a reminder on my calendar." In that sentence, had means owned. It is not the regret form. A third line is, "I wish I were on the list." Were is the form we use after wish when we mean now.

Then say a wish about the past. "I wish I had asked the tutor." The asking is finished, and you are sorry you did not do it. Do not say, "I wish I would have asked." After wish, a past regret uses had plus the past participle. Had asked, had set, and had signed are the forms for tonight.

One different past is enough. "If I had asked, I would have known." The if half uses had plus a participle. The other half uses would have plus a participle. You do not need every person, and you do not need both clause orders. One clear sentence is the goal. Chris can say, "If I had set an alarm, I would have arrived on time."

You can put the same idea in a shorter line. "I should have asked earlier." That line is one row in the grammar box. It is not a new lesson. It means the same thing as the wish about the past. Use it once, then move to the next step.

Next time, make a plan you can do. "Next time I will ask on the first day." You can also say, "If I had another chance, I would ask on the first day." Put a reminder on the calendar. Set an alarm the day before. Bring one question to practice. If you are not sure which choice to make, ask at the help desk.

sections.html:
Read across. The left side is the sentence. The right side is the meaning.

Grammar Box 1: unless means if not

SENTENCEMEANING
You can't go in unless you sign the book.if you do not sign
You can't go in unless you call first.if you do not call
Unless you confirm, they will not hold the room.present verb after unless

Grammar Box 2: as long as

SENTENCEMEANING
You can bring a guest as long as you tell the desk.only if you tell them
You can wait as long as the group finishes on time.only if that stays true
As long as you call first, they will hold the room.present verb, same as if

Grammar Box 3: even though

SENTENCEMEANING
Even though the office is busy, you still need an appointment.the result happens anyway
Even though you are on time, you still need to confirm.on time does not change the rule
Even though you have permission, you still sign the book.permission is not enough

Grammar Box 4: have to, must, and if

SENTENCEMEANING
You have to sign the book.a requirement
You must wear the visitor badge.a requirement
If you call first, they will hold the room.if + present, then will

Rule of thumb: unless means if… not. As long as means "only if this stays true." Even though means the result happens anyway.

Questions and answers

Q: Can I say Unless you will call?

A: No. Use the present: Unless you call.

Q: What does as long as mean?

A: Only if this stays true.

Q: What does even though mean?

A: The result happens anyway.

Practice A: Write unless, as long as, or even though.

Practice B: Circle the correct words.

  1. Unless you (call / will call) first, you can't go in.
  2. As long as you (tell / will tell) the desk, you can bring a guest.
  3. Even though he is on time, he (still must / doesn't) confirm.
  4. You (must / must to) wear the visitor badge.
  5. If you call first, they (hold / will hold) the room.
  6. You have to sign (unless / even though) you already have permission.

✗ Don't say✓ Say
Unless you will call, they will not hold the room.Unless you call, they will not hold the room.
As long as you will tell them, you can bring a guest.As long as you tell them, you can bring a guest.

You must to wear the badge.You must wear the visitor badge.

A. Read the policy and the notice. Read fast first. Then read again and answer the questions.

VISITOR POLICY · a class example

Please read this policy before you go to the front desk. The office and the rules on this page are invented for class.

A visitor needs an appointment. You can't go in unless you call first. Call the front desk during office hours. Office hours are nine to five, Monday to Friday. If you call first, the front desk will hold the room until your time. Unless you confirm, they will not hold the room.

When you arrive, you have to sign the book. Write your name and the time. You must wear a visitor badge. Wear the badge where people can see it. Give it back at the front desk when you leave. A badge is not a key. It only shows that you signed in.

You can bring one guest as long as you tell the front desk before you come. Tell them the guest's name. The guest has to sign the book. The guest must wear a badge too. You cannot bring a guest unless the desk says yes. Two guests are too many for one visit.

Even though the office is busy, you still need an appointment. Even though you are on time, you still need to confirm. A busy lobby does not change the rule. A call the day before is best. A call the same morning is OK as long as someone answers the phone.

There is one exception. A worker who already has permission from the front desk may walk a visitor to the desk. The visitor still has to sign the book and wear a badge. Permission is not the same as an appointment. Unless you confirm, the desk cannot make an exception for a meeting room. The exception is for the walk to the desk, not for the room.

If you need to cancel, call the front desk. Say your name and the time. Do not ask a friend to cancel for you unless you cannot call. If you do not understand a requirement, ask one polite question. You can say, "What happens unless I call?" The person at the desk will point to the notice and explain the rule.

Keep the policy near the door. Read the notice again if you are not sure. The front desk can repeat a rule. They cannot change the policy during your visit. Write the two rules you need in a note to a coworker, and ask the desk if a word is not clear.

BUILDING NOTICE · six lines

  1. Office hours are nine to five.
  2. You can't go in unless you sign the book.
  3. You must wear a visitor badge.
  4. You can wait in the lobby as long as a meeting is still in the room.
  5. Even though the lobby is open, the offices close at five.
  6. Ask the front desk if you do not understand a rule.

  2. What must a visitor wear? ______________________________________________
  3. When can you bring a guest? ______________________________________________
  4. What are the office hours? ______________________________________________
  5. Who explains a rule? ______________________________________________

Example: You can't go in unless you call first. You have to sign the book. You must wear a visitor badge. You can bring a guest as long as you tell the front desk. Even though the office is busy, you still need an appointment. If you are not sure, ask the front desk.

How to Use This Plan

Teach in English. You do not need to speak the learner's language. Show, point, and gesture. There is no contrast box on the student page. The common mix-up is in the mistakes table, in English.

Instructions: use the same short task words every week: Listen. Circle. Check. Write. Work with a partner. Work in a group. Ask a follow-up question. Give a reason.

Instruction rule: Model it (do it with one learner while everyone watches), check it (ask: "Does unless mean if or if not?"), then go. Say less, show more.

Grouping toolkit: Pairs: turn to a neighbor; with an odd number, make one group of 3. Groups: 3–4 learners. The teacher joins a pair only if one learner is left over.

When a learner is stuck: (1) show the picture, a gesture, or the board; (2) give one more short English example; (3) point to the grammar box; (4) a classmate can help for a few seconds, then back to English.

About four sentences: in Level 5, the Talk Time product and the exit ticket are about four connected sentences. Opening Talk is shorter: two or three sentences, then one follow-up.

Lesson 4 (Week 4): Unless You Call First

At a glance

Objectives: learners can…

  • explain unless in their own words
  • say what is allowed as long as something else is true
  • contrast with even though
  • ask one polite question about a rule they do not understand

Materials

  • Student Pages for Lesson 4 (print for the number expected + 3 spares)
  • Board and markers
  • Six rule strips (copy the strips from the Talk Time page, one set per pair)
  • Listening: phone + small speaker, L5_L4_listening.mp3 (1:48). No speaker? Read the script aloud with a volunteer.
  • Prep time: 15 minutes (read the plan; cut the strips; practice reading the listening script).

Key vocabulary (with pictures on the New Words page)

★ policy • ★ notice • ★ appointment • ★ cancel • ★ confirm • ★ visitor • ★ front desk • ★ office hours • ★ requirement • ★ permission • exception • visitor badge

Also: sign the book, hold the room, a guest, a lobby, office hours from nine to five.

Clock-time plan

Times are loose. If the listening or Talk Time runs long, take the time from Read & Write.

Attendance (15 → 7–8 → 5 or fewer): with 5 or fewer, the whole group sorts the strips, then pairs ask. Late arrivals join any pair right away.

Step by step

Step 1 · 6:00–6:06 · Opening Talk · 6 min

  • Grouping: pairs. 15 learners: 7 pairs + 1 group of 3. 7–8 learners: 3–4 pairs. 5 or fewer: pairs, or one group with you.
  • Say this once: "This lesson is not legal advice. For a real question about your job or your building, ask that office, or use the local help line on the Keep practicing sheet."
  • Before class: write on the board: unless = if not and You can't go in unless you call first.
  • Opening Talk (5 min): learners open the Opening Talk page. A asks a card question; B answers in two or three sentences; A asks one follow-up. Switch after each card.
  • Model with one learner: you ask, "What do you wish you had asked last week?" The learner answers. Then you ask, "Why?" Help them stop after two or three sentences.
  • Card 4 is the homework check: one I wish I had sentence from last week. Do not ask about family loss, money trouble, or leaving a country.
  • If behind: one card only.

Step 2 · 6:06–6:12 · New Words · 6 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the New Words page.
  • Do: point to each picture and say the word. Learners repeat once. ★ = the most important words.
  • Show the hard words: appointment (a set time) vs. permission (someone says you may); confirm (the time is yes) vs. cancel (the time is off); requirement (you have to) vs. exception (one time, not the usual rule). Office hours on the card are nine to five.
  • Check the meaning (1 min): "Does unless mean if or if not?" (if not) • "What must a visitor wear?" (a visitor badge) • "Where do you ask about a rule?" (the front desk).
  • Partner game (2 min): A points to a picture and asks a question. B answers. Switch. Example: "visitor: What does a visitor wear?" "A visitor badge."
  • If behind: teach the ★ words only.

Step 3 · 6:12–6:32 · Listening + "Hear it, say it" · 20 min

  • Grouping: individuals, then pairs check. With 5 or fewer, check together as a group.
  • Before you listen (2 min): say: "Andre did not call first. Helen explains the rule, and Mei says he can wait. Listen: can he go in now?"
  • Voices: Andre, Helen, and Mei. A narrator opens and closes the audio.
  • Play 1 → Task A (the main idea). Pairs compare. Check together. Then read Tasks B and C together so learners know what to listen for.
  • Play 2 → Tasks B and C. Pairs compare. Then show the answers (answer key).
  • "Hear it, say it" (3 min): gonna and wanna are short forms. This listening uses the full forms. You can say want to and going to. Then say unless with stress on the second syllable, and say as long as as one chunk. The class repeats each line two times.
  • The audio plays the conversation once (1:48). Press play again for play 2. A third play is fine if the class needs it. The script says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna; learners only need to recognize those words.
  • If behind: do Task C together on the board, reading the lines yourself.

Step 4 · 6:32–6:45 · Grammar Q&A · 13 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the Grammar page. The left side is the sentence. The right side is the meaning.
  • Show it (2 min): on the board, write if you do not call and draw an arrow to unless you call. Say both. Then say as long as as "only if this stays true," and even though as "the result happens anyway."
  • The boxes: Box 1 unless. Box 2 as long as. Box 3 even though. Box 4 have to, must, and if + will.
  • Rule of thumb (read it aloud): unless means if… not. As long as means "only if this stays true." Even though means the result happens anyway.
  • Questions and answers: Q: Can I say Unless you will call? A: No. Use the present: Unless you call. Q: What does as long as mean? A: Only if this stays true. Q: What does even though mean? A: The result happens anyway.
  • Practice A and B: learners write, then pairs check. Go over the answers. Read the Common mistakes table together: "Don't say… Say…".
  • Pair check (last 2 min): A reads a rule strip. B says unless, as long as, or even though. Switch.
  • If behind: skip the pair check. Talk Time practices it.

Break · 6:45–7:00 · 15 min

  • Write on the board: unless = if not · as long as = only if this stays true · even though = the result happens anyway.

Step 5 · 7:00–7:18 · Talk Time: Notice Sort + Ask the Desk · 18 min

  • Model it first (1 min): hold up "You can't go in unless you call first." Ask: "Which word?" (unless). Then ask one learner, "What happens unless I call?" Answer with the rule.
  • Round 1 (8 min): Notice Sort (pairs). Pairs get six rule strips and match each one to unless, as long as, or even though. They say the rule in their own words.
  • Round 2 (8 min): Ask the Desk (pairs). A is the front desk. B asks one question about a rule (What happens unless I call?). A answers with unless, as long as, or even though. Switch.
  • 15 learners: pairs, then a new partner. 7–8: pairs. 5 or fewer: the whole group sorts the strips, then pairs ask.
  • Do not role-play evictions, firings, or punishments. The notices are invented.
  • If behind: round 1 only.

Step 6 · 7:18–7:25 · Read & Write: A visitor policy + a note · 7 min

  • Grouping: pairs read and answer; individual writing. With 5 or fewer, read the notice aloud together.
  • Read (4 min): learners read the visitor policy and the six-line building notice. Say: "Read fast first. Then find the answers." Pairs answer questions 1–5 together.
  • Check (1 min): go over the answers (answer key).
  • Write (2 min, finish at home): a 6-sentence note to a coworker explaining two rules, with unless and as long as. Invented details are fine.
  • If behind: questions 1–5 only; the writing becomes homework.

Step 7 · 7:25–7:30 · Exit Ticket + Homework · 5 min · NEVER SKIP

  • Exit ticket (3 min): Explain one rule from tonight. Four sentences: the rule, unless or as long as, an example, and who to ask if you are not sure. With 5 or fewer, a learner can say it to you first and then write it.
  • Collect the pages. After class, sort them into ✓ / almost / not yet. Start next week with 2 corrections on the board (no names).
  • Homework (2 min): about 15–20 minutes. Item 1 is three sentences, one with each new word. Item 2 finishes the note. Item 3 is one polite question about a class rule, not a real job problem. Item 4 reviews have to and must.

Narrator: Lesson four. Andre is at the front desk. He wants to go to a meeting, but he did not call first.

Helen: Good afternoon. Do you have an appointment?

Andre: I want to go to the four o'clock meeting. I did not call this morning.

Helen: I'm sorry. You can't go in unless you call first. That rule is on the notice.

Andre: Even though I am on time?

Helen: Even though you are on time, you still need to confirm.

Andre: What do I have to do?

Helen: You have to sign the book, and you must wear a visitor badge.

Andre: Is there an exception if I already have permission?

Helen: Permission is not the same as an appointment. Unless you confirm, the desk cannot make an exception.

Helen: The requirement is on the door. Please read the policy before you sit down.

Mei: Hi, Andre. You can wait as long as the four o'clock group finishes on time.

Andre: What happens unless they finish?

Mei: Then the room is closed. If you call first next time, they will hold the room.

Helen: You can bring a guest as long as you tell the front desk.

Andre: I am going to call tomorrow. Can I cancel today's meeting?

Helen: Yes. I can cancel it, or you can wait. Office hours end at five.

Andre: What happens unless I call tomorrow too?

Mei: Call during office hours, from nine to five. Then they can confirm the room.

  • Listening Task B: 1 false, 2 true, 3 true, 4 true, 5 false, 6 true.
  • Listening Task C: 1 unless, 2 Even though, 3 as long as, 4 as long as, 5 Unless, 6 unless.
  • Grammar Practice A: 1 unless, 2 as long as, 3 Even though, 4 Unless, 5 even though, 6 as long as.
  • Grammar Practice B: 1 call, 2 tell, 3 still must, 4 must, 5 will hold, 6 even though.
  • Talk Time, Notice Sort: 1 unless, 2 as long as, 3 even though, 4 unless, 5 as long as, 6 even though. Ask the Desk: answers will vary.

  • Read & Write B: 1 No. Call first. • 2 A visitor badge. • 3 Tell the front desk first. • 4 Nine to five. • 5 The front desk. • Writing (C): answers will vary.
  • Exit ticket: answers will vary. A good answer: "You can't go in unless you call first. As long as you tell the front desk, you can bring a guest. For example, call in the morning and give your name. If you are not sure, ask the front desk."

  • The three words: unless = if not. As long as = only if this stays true. Even though = the result happens anyway. After unless, as long as, and if, the verb for a future meaning stays present: unless you call, not unless you will call.
  • Reductions: the listening says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna. Learners only need to recognize the short forms; they can always say the full forms.

A. Read. Read once. Then find the answers.

Phone log · Monday 2:10

This page is a practice phone log. It is not medical advice. It does not name a symptom, a medicine, or a test result. The only news is a new day and time for a checkup. For a real health question, ask your clinic. In an emergency, call 911.

Phone log. Monday, 2:10. Nurse Patel called Jana, and Jana called back. The nurse said, "The checkup is on Thursday." She told Jana that the time had changed. She asked Jana to call before 3:00. She asked Jana to bring the appointment card. She asked if Thursday was OK. Jana said yes.

The nurse also said, "We will call you if the room changes." When Jana reports that sentence later, will becomes would. She said they would call her if the room changes. Say does not need a person. Tell does. Jana can say, "She told me the time had changed." She should not say, "She said me," and she should not say, "She told to me."

The call ends before Jana goes home. At home, she tells her brother Ken. Ken was not on the clinic call. Jana is the person who passes the message on. A message needs three details so another person can act: who called, what day, and what to do.

Here is the message Jana would leave. "The nurse said the checkup was on Thursday. She told me the time had changed. She asked me to call before 3:00. She asked me to bring the appointment card. She asked if Thursday was OK. She said they would call me if the room changes."

Ken reads it back. He can say who, what day, and what to do. Who: Nurse Patel. Day: Thursday. What to do: call before 3:00 and bring the appointment card. If one of those is missing, the message is not enough. Add the missing line. Do not add a symptom. There is no symptom in this log.

Write the message in six to eight sentences. Use said or told, asked me to, and asked if. The quote can be the practice message. It should not be a classmate's private life. Keep the note in the folder. Write the callback number only if it is the invented number on this page.

Read across. The left side is the question. The right side is the answer.

Grammar Box 1: a negative tag

QUESTIONANSWER
You sent the form, didn't you?Yes, I did.
The class is on Tuesday, isn't it?Yes, it is.
She signed the copy, didn't she?Yes, she did.

A positive statement takes a negative tag. The falling tone means you are checking, not starting an argument.

Grammar Box 2: a positive tag

QUESTIONANSWER
She isn't on the list, is she?No, she isn't.
The room isn't A, is it?No, it isn't.
You didn't initial it, did you?Actually, I did.

A negative statement takes a positive tag.

Grammar Box 3: do, does, or did

QUESTIONANSWER
You need a copy, don't you?Yes, I do.
The schedule starts at six, doesn't it?Yes, it does.
Leah checked the spelling, didn't she?Yes, she did.

Rule of thumb: The tag uses the same helping verb as the statement, and it flips the yes/no. If there is no helping verb, use do / does / did.

Grammar Box 4: correct a detail

QUESTIONANSWER
The room is A, isn't it?Actually, it's room C.
The class is on Wednesday, isn't it?Actually, it's on Tuesday.
Your email ends in mail.example, doesn't it?Yes, it does.

Questions and answers

Q: The person says yes. Can I answer Yes, I didn't?

A: No. If the answer is yes, the short answer stays positive: Yes, I did.

Q: I am sure, and I only want to check. Do I say You sent it, did you?

A: No. The check on a positive sentence takes didn't: You sent it, didn't you?

Q: The statement is negative. What tag do I use?

A: A positive tag. She isn't on the list, is she?

How to Use This Plan

Teach in English. Show, point, and gesture. The common mix-up is a row in the mistakes table. There is no separate tip to translate.

Instructions: use the same short task words every week: Listen. Circle. Check. Write. Work with a partner. Work in a group. Ask a follow-up question. Give a reason.

Instruction rule: Model it (do it with one learner while everyone watches), check it (ask: "Positive statement or negative? What tag?"), then go. Say less, show more.

Grouping toolkit: Pairs: turn to a neighbor; with an odd number, make one group of 3. Groups: 3–4 learners. The teacher joins a pair only if one learner is left over.

When a learner is stuck: (1) show it: the picture, a gesture, or the board; (2) give one more short English example; (3) point to the grammar box; (4) a classmate can help for a few seconds, then back to English.

Four sentences on the exit ticket: two of them are tags, and one is a correction or one Yes, it is.

Lesson 7 (Week 7): You Sent It, Didn't You?

At a glance

By the end of class, you can do these four things.

Today you will: Add a tag to a statement I think is true. Answer a tag with a short yes or no. Write a confirmation email.

Now you can: Add a tag to a statement I think is true. Answer a tag with a short yes or no. Write a confirmation email.

Objectives: learners can…

  • I can add a tag to a statement I think is true.
  • I can answer a tag with a short yes or no.
  • I can correct a wrong detail politely.
  • I can write a confirmation email.

Materials

  • Student Pages for Lesson 7 (print for the number expected + 3 spares)
  • Board and markers
  • Two copies of the Detail Check form on the Talk Time page (one says Tuesday; one says Wednesday)
  • Listening: phone + small speaker. The audio is recorded (about 1:30). No speaker? Read the script aloud with a volunteer.
  • Prep time: 15 minutes (read the plan; mark one wrong detail on a desk copy; practice the falling tag).

Key vocabulary (with pictures on the New Words page)

★ spelling • ★ email address • ★ phone number • ★ schedule • ★ signature • ★ form • ★ checkbox • ★ correction • ★ double-check • ★ copy • initial • capital letter

Also: class ID, confirm, mismatch, evening class, community center desk.

Clock-time plan

Times are loose. If the listening or Talk Time runs long, take the time from Read & Write.

Attendance (15 → 7–8 → 5 or fewer): with 5 or fewer, sit at one table. For Talk Time, use one form, and you read a wrong detail.

Step by step

Step 1 · 6:00–6:06 · Opening Talk + Homework Check · 6 min

  • Grouping: pairs, the same partner for both parts. 15 learners: 7 pairs + 1 group of 3. 7–8 learners: 3–4 pairs. 5 or fewer: pairs, or one group with you.
  • Before class: write on the board: She said… / She told me… / She asked me to… / She asked if…
  • Opening Talk: A asks last week's question. B answers with a short summary. The quote can be from Lesson 6, not from a classmate's private life.
  • Model with one learner: "The nurse said the checkup was on Thursday. She told me the time had changed. She asked me to call before 3:00. She asked if Thursday was OK."
  • Homework Check: pairs read one sentence from the Lesson 6 message. Write 2 corrections on the board (often said me and told that). No names.
  • If behind: one card only.

Step 2 · 6:06–6:12 · New Words · 6 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the New Words page.
  • Do: point to each picture and say the word. Learners repeat once. ★ = the most important words.
  • Show the hard words: email address (not the message, the address) • signature (your name in writing) vs. initial (the first letters only) • checkbox (a small box you mark) • double-check (look a second time) • capital letter (L, not l).
  • Check the Meaning: 1. Is this a phone number or an email address? (an email address) • 2. What small box do you mark on a form? (a checkbox) • 3. Is the L in Leah small or capital? (capital).
  • Partner game: Check the form! A points to a picture. B names it and uses it in one sentence. Switch. 15 learners: then 3 teams. 7–8: 2 teams. 5 or fewer: one team against the clock.
  • If behind: teach the ★ words only.

Step 3 · 6:12–6:32 · Listening + "Hear it, say it" · 20 min

  • Grouping: individuals, then pairs check. With 5 or fewer, check together as a group.
  • Before you listen: "Leah is at a community center desk. She wants to check her evening-class form with Mr. Ortiz. Listen: is every detail correct at the start?"
  • Voices: Narrator, Leah, Mr. Ortiz.
  • Play 1 → Task A (the main idea). Pairs compare. Check together.
  • Read Tasks B and C together so learners know what to listen for.
  • Play 2 → Tasks B and C. Pairs compare. Then show the answers.
  • "Hear it, say it": gonna and wanna are short forms. This listening uses the full forms. You can say going to and want to. Say each line two times. The tag falls when you are only checking. A rising tag can mean a real question. This lesson practices the falling check.
  • The audio is recorded (about 1:30). When it is ready, it plays the conversation once. Press play again for play 2. A third play is fine if the class needs it. Until then, read the script with a volunteer at a normal, friendly speed, two times.
  • If behind: do Task C together on the board.

Step 4 · 6:32–6:45 · Grammar Q&A + pair check · 13 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. The left side is the question. The right side is the answer.
  • Show it: say a sure detail with a falling tag: "You sent the form, didn't you?" Nod on didn't you. Then shake your head and say, "Actually, the room is C."
  • The boxes: Box 1 positive statement, negative tag. Box 2 negative statement, positive tag. Box 3 no helping verb, so do / does / did. Box 4 Actually plus the right detail.
  • Rule of thumb: The tag uses the same helping verb as the statement, and it flips the yes/no. If there is no helping verb, use do / does / did.
  • Questions and answers: read each Q. The class reads the A.
  • Practice A and B: learners write, then pairs check. Read the Common mistakes table: "Don't say… Say…"
  • Pair check: A says, "The room is A." B adds the tag: "The room is A, isn't it?" A answers, "Actually, it's room C." Then switch. 15 learners: swap partners once if time. 5 or fewer: you join one pair.
  • If behind: skip the pair check. Talk Time practices it.

Break · 6:45–7:00 · 15 min

  • Write on the board: Positive statement → negative tag. Negative statement → positive tag. Yes stays yes: Yes, I did.

Step 5 · 7:00–7:18 · Talk Time: Detail Check + Read-Back · 18 min

  • Model it first: hold up the Tuesday copy and the Wednesday copy. Ask, "It's Tuesday, isn't it?" Answer, "Actually, it's Wednesday."
  • Round 1, Detail Check (pairs): A has a form with four details. B has a slightly different copy. They confirm with tags and correct one item. 15: pairs, swap forms once. 7–8: pairs. 5 or fewer: one form, and you read a wrong detail.
  • Round 2, Read-Back: B says a two-sentence confirmation. A listens and answers the tag. Then switch.
  • The forms use a class ID only. Do not collect real Social Security numbers, immigration papers, bank numbers, or medical record numbers. Praise the correction, not the speed.
  • If behind: round 1 only.

Step 6 · 7:18–7:25 · Read & Write · 7 min

  • Grouping: pairs read and answer; individual writing. With 5 or fewer, read the email aloud together.
  • Read: the registration form and Mr. Ortiz's email. One detail does not match. Say: "Read fast first. Then find the mismatch."
  • Check: go over questions 1–5.
  • Write: a confirmation email of 6–8 sentences that names the mismatch and the correction. This is writing check 3. Learners start in class and finish at home. After class, write one strength and one fix. No grade on the person, only on the email.
  • If behind: questions 1–5 only; the writing becomes homework.

Step 7 · 7:25–7:30 · Exit Ticket + Homework · 5 min · NEVER SKIP

  • Exit ticket: Confirm two details about this class. Four sentences, two of them tags, and one correction or one Yes, it is. Example: The class is on Tuesday, isn't it? Yes, it is. The room is A, isn't it? Actually, it's room C.
  • Collect the pages. Sort them into yes / almost / not yet. Start next week with 2 corrections. No names.
  • Homework: about 20–25 minutes. Do item 1 together: You sent the form, ______? → You sent the form, didn't you?

Listening script

1:30. The conversation plays once, so press play again for the second listen.

Audio: Play L5_L7_listening.mp3 (1:30) from a phone and a small speaker. No speaker? Read the script with a volunteer, at a normal, friendly speed. The script says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna; learners only need to recognize those words.

Narrator: Lesson seven. Leah is at the community center desk. She wants to check her evening-class form. Mr. Ortiz has the copy.

Mr. Ortiz: Good evening. You sent the form, didn't you?

Leah: Yes, I did. I want to double-check every line.

Mr. Ortiz: Your class ID is C42, isn't it?

Leah: Yes, it is.

Mr. Ortiz: And the email address is right, isn't it?

Leah: Yes, it is. The name starts with a capital letter. Please check the spelling.

Mr. Ortiz: I will. You wrote a phone number on line three, didn't you?

Leah: Yes, I did. I double-checked it at home.

Mr. Ortiz: The class is on Tuesday at six, isn't it?

Leah: Yes, it is. I'm going to come straight from work.

Mr. Ortiz: And the room is A, isn't it?

Leah: Actually, it isn't. The schedule says room C. Can you make that correction?

Mr. Ortiz: You're right. I'll change the room to C and initial the correction.

Leah: Thank you. My signature is on the form, isn't it?

Mr. Ortiz: Yes, it is. I'll check the box and give you this copy.

Leah: Great. I'm going to keep the copy.

Mr. Ortiz: Your friend isn't in this class, is she?

Narrator: That's the end of the listening.

Answer key

  • Listening Task A: b (No. The room is wrong.)
  • Listening Task B: 1 Correct, 2 Correct, 3 Correct, 4 Correct, 5 Wrong. C42 is the class ID. Tuesday at six is 6:00. The room on his copy is A; the schedule says room C.
  • Listening Task C: 1 didn't you, 2 isn't it, 3 isn't it, 4 didn't you, 5 isn't it, 6 is she.
  • Grammar Practice A: 1 didn't you, 2 isn't it, 3 is she, 4 don't you, 5 doesn't it, 6 didn't she.
  • Grammar Practice B: 1 Yes, I did. 2 isn't it, 3 is she, 4 didn't you, 5 isn't it, 6 No, I didn't.
  • Talk Time: answers will vary. One good correction: It's Tuesday, isn't it? Actually, it's Wednesday.
  • Homework 1: 1 You sent the form, didn't you? 2 The class is on Tuesday, isn't it? 3 She isn't on the list, is she? 4 You need a copy, don't you? Homework 2–4: answers will vary. A good item 4: She told me to check the room.
  • Read & Write B: 1 C-42. 2 Tuesday at 6:00. 3 Room C. 4 Room A. 5 The room. Writing (C): answers will vary. A good email names room A and room C and asks for the correction.
  • Exit ticket: answers will vary. A good answer: "The class is on Tuesday, isn't it? Yes, it is. The room is A, isn't it? Actually, it's room C."

Teacher notes

  • The forms use a class ID, an email, and an invented phone number. Do not collect real Social Security numbers, immigration papers, bank numbers, or medical record numbers.
  • Praise the correction, not the speed. Actually plus the right detail is the goal.
  • Falling tag: you are checking, not starting an argument. Mention that a rising tag can mean a real question. Practice only the falling check tonight.
  • Reductions: the listening says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna. Learners only need to recognize the short forms.

sections.title: Grammar
sections.html:
Read across. The left side is the question. The right side is the answer.

Grammar Box 1: if or whether

QUESTIONANSWER
Do you know if the conference is tonight?Yes. It starts at 6:30. / I'm not sure.
Do you know whether I need a permission slip?Yes. Please bring the slip.
Can you tell me if the office is still open?Yes. It closes at seven.

Grammar Box 2: when or where

QUESTIONANSWER
Do you know where the office is?It's down the hallway, by the office window.
Do you know when it starts?It starts at 6:30.
Do you know where I sign up?At the office window.

Grammar Box 3: said or told

QUESTIONANSWER
What did he say about the night?He said the conference was tonight.
What did he tell you to bring?He told me to bring the slip.
What did he say about the time?He said it starts at 6:30.

Grammar Box 4: statement order

NOT THISSAY THIS
Do you know if is the conference tonight?Do you know if the conference is tonight?
Do you know where is the office?Do you know where the office is?
Do you know when does it start?Do you know when it starts?

Rule of thumb: After Do you know if / whether / when / where, use statement order. Not Do you know if is the conference tonight?

Q: Can I say Do you know if is the office open?

A: No. Statement order: Do you know if the office is open?

Q: Can I say Do you know where is the conference?

A: No. Do you know where the conference is?

Q: How do I report the answer?

Lesson 8 (Week 9): Do You Know If It's Tonight?

At a glance

Today you will: Ask Do you know if / whether…? Keep statement order after if. Report the answer with said or told.

Now you can: Ask Do you know if / whether…? Keep statement order after if. Report the answer with said or told.

Objectives: learners can…

  • I can ask Do you know if / whether…?
  • I can keep statement order after if.

Listening script

1:43. The conversation plays once, so press play again for the second listen.

Audio: Play L5_L8_listening.mp3 (1:43) from a phone and a small speaker. No speaker? Read the script with a volunteer, at a normal, friendly speed. The script says going to and want to. People often say gonna and wanna; learners only need to recognize those words.

Narrator: Lesson eight. Maya is calling the office at Northside School. She volunteers for the after-school reading hour. Mr. Reed answers the phone.

Mr. Reed: Northside School office. This is Mr. Reed.

Maya: Hello. This is Maya. I want to ask about the conference.

Mr. Reed: Of course. How can I help you?

Maya: Do you know if the conference is tonight?

Mr. Reed: Yes. It starts at six thirty, in the library.

Maya: Thank you. Do you know whether I should bring the signup sheet?

Mr. Reed: Yes. Please bring the signup sheet. I'm going to set it by the office window.

Maya: Do you know where the office window is?

Mr. Reed: It's down the hallway, past the bell.

Maya: Can you tell me if I need a permission slip? I'm a volunteer, not a parent.

Mr. Reed: A volunteer does not need a slip. A parent brings a permission slip for early pickup.

Maya: Do you know when I should arrive?

Mr. Reed: Please arrive ten minutes early.

Maya: I will. I'm going to put the sheet in my backpack.

Maya: Do you know where I should leave my backpack?

Mr. Reed: Leave it by the office window.

Mr. Reed: The newsletter also says the conference is tonight.

Maya: Do you know if dismissal is at the usual time?

Mr. Reed: Yes. Dismissal is at three. The conference is in the evening.

Maya: Thank you. I don't want to miss the start.

Mr. Reed: You're welcome. We'll see you ten minutes early.

Narrator: That's the end of the listening.

  • Check the Meaning: 1 a backpack, 2 a bell, 3 a permission slip.
  • Listening Task A: b (to ask about the conference).
  • Listening Task B: 1 tonight, 2 6:30, 3 the signup sheet, 4 ten minutes early, 5 down the hallway, 6 no. Six thirty in the script is 6:30.
  • Listening Task C: 1 if, 2 whether, 3 where, 4 if, 5 if, 6 where.
  • Grammar Practice A: 1 where, 2 when, 3 whether, 4 if, 5 where, 6 when.
  • Grammar Practice B: 1 the conference is, 2 the office is, 3 it starts, 4 said, 5 me, 6 the office is.

Read across. The left side is the clue. The right side is what you say.

Grammar Box 1: must be

CLUEANSWER
The page has a Buy now button. What is it?It must be an ad.
The store's page says the store is open. What is the closing post?It must be a rumor.
The logo, the author, and the date all match. What is the page?It must be the store's page.

Must means you are almost sure.

Grammar Box 2: might be

CLUEANSWER
The date says 2019. What do you think?It might be old.
There is no author. What do you think?It might be a rumor.
The comment has no source. What do you think?It might be a guess.

Might is a guess you are less sure about.

Grammar Box 3: can't be

CLUEANSWER
The logo is different. Is it the city's page?It can't be the city's page.
The store's page says open. Is the store closing?It can't be closing.
The first post has no author and no date. Is it a fact?It can't be a fact.

Grammar Box 4: how sure?

HOW SURE?SAY
You are almost sure.must be
You are less sure.might be
It is not possible.can't be

Rule of thumb: must / might / can't + be or another base verb. Can't here means "that is not possible," not "is not able."

Narrator: Lesson nine. Noah shows Aisha a post. The post says their grocery store is closing. They want to check the source.

Noah: Aisha, please look at this post. It says our grocery store is closing on Friday.

Aisha: Do you know who wrote it? I don't see an author.

Noah: There is no author. And I don't see a date stamp.

Aisha: Then it might be old. It might be a rumor. I'm going to look for the store's own page.

Noah: Here it is. The logo matches our store.

Aisha: What does that page say?

Noah: It says the store is open. The hours are the same.

Aisha: Then the closing post can't be true. It must be a rumor.

Aisha: Don't share it yet. We want to check a second source first.

Noah: The store page names the author. The author is the store. The date is this week.

Aisha: That page must be the one we trust. The first post has no author and no date.

Noah: So the store isn't closing. I'm not going to share the post.

Aisha: Good. It can't be a fact when the store's own page says the opposite.

Noah: There is a comment under the post, but the comment has no source.

Aisha: A comment is not a fact. It might be someone's guess.

Noah: I see. A reliable page names the author and the date.

Aisha: Yes. And it matches a second source. This one does.

sections.title: Grammar
sections.html:
Read across. The left side is the pattern. The right side is the example.

Grammar Box 1: a middle idea

YOU CAN SAYA MIDDLE IDEA
What if we split the day?I can take the morning if you take the afternoon.
Let's meet in the middle.We can swap at twelve.
Say the other idea first.You need the afternoon. I need the morning.

Grammar Box 2: so… that / such… that

PATTERNEXAMPLE
so + adjective + thatThe week was so busy that we split Saturday.
such + a + adjective + noun + thatIt was such a long shift that we shared it.
so + adjective + thatThe visit is so important that Jon needs the afternoon.
such + a + adjective + noun + thatNoon is such a clear time that nobody has to guess.

Grammar Box 3: work out, call off, give in (review)

REVIEWA REAL SENTENCE
work it outWe can work it out.
call it offShe is not going to call it off.
call the shift offNoun after, or it in the middle: call it off.
give inWe didn't give in. No object.

Grammar Box 4: don't mix them

DON'T MIX THEMSAY
so + adjective + thatThe week was so busy that we split Saturday.
such a + adjective + nounIt was such a long shift that we shared it.
too + adjective + forThe week is too full for one person.

Rule of thumb: Say the other person's idea in one sentence before you offer yours. So and such both mean the result was big enough to cause the next clause.

Q: Can I say so busy so we split it?

A: No. Say so busy that we split it.

Q: So or such before a long shift?

A: Such. It was such a long shift.

Q: Can I say give in the argument?

A: No. Give in has no object here.

Don't saySay

Camila: I want to take the morning off. I have a class, and that class is my priority.

Jon: I hear you. I have a family visit in the afternoon. I was going to ask for the whole day too.

Ms. Nguyen: Say the other person's idea before you offer yours.

Camila: Jon, you need the afternoon for a family visit. I need the morning for my class.

Jon: Yes. What if we split the day? I can take the morning if you take the afternoon.

Camila: That is a fair offer. My class ends at noon. What if we swap at twelve? That is my counteroffer.

Jon: Your counteroffer works. The week was so busy that we split Saturday.

Camila: And it was such a long shift that we shared it. The week is too full for one person.

Jon: The visit is so important that I need the afternoon. This solution is about fairness.

Camila: My class is so important that I need the morning. We didn't give in. We found the middle.

Jon: I'll write the shared task on a sticky note and put it on the whiteboard.

Camila: We each get a break time. I'm going to come in at noon.

Ms. Nguyen: Read the compromise, please. I want to hear it.

Jon: I'm going to work the morning. Camila is going to work the afternoon. We swap at twelve.

Camila: Noon is such a clear time that nobody has to guess.

Ms. Nguyen: You worked it out. I'm not going to call it off. Thank you for the compromise.

Narrator: That's the end of the listening.

Answer key

  • Listening Task A: b (Both need Saturday off.)
  • Listening Task B: 1 a morning class, 2 an afternoon visit, 3 twelve, 4 such a long shift, 5 a sticky note, 6 not call it off.
  • Listening Task C: 1 so, 2 such, 3 so, 4 such, 5 so, 6 so.
  • Grammar Practice A: 1 so, 2 such, 3 too, 4 so, 5 such, 6 it out.
  • Grammar Practice B: 1 so, 2 such, 3 it out, 4 it off, 5 give in, 6 too.
  • Talk Time: answers will vary. A good compromise names both needs and one middle time.
  • Homework 1: The week was so busy that we split Saturday. Homework 2–4: answers will vary.
  • Read & Write: 1 The Saturday shift. 2 A morning class. 3 At noon. 4 On the whiteboard. 5 No. She will not call it off.
  • Exit ticket: answers will vary. A good answer has four sentences: each person's need, the middle idea, a so / such result, and why it was fair.

Teacher notes

  • The conflict is a schedule between coworkers, not a complaint against a boss and not a pay dispute. Ms. Nguyen only asks them to decide. Do not role-play yelling.
  • Praise the sentence that repeats the other person's need.
  • Give in the argument is the wrong pattern. Give in has no object here.
  • Work it out and call it off: it only in the middle. You can also put the noun after: call the shift off.
  • Invented limits are fine. Do not ask about real pay, a real boss, or a real family problem.
  • gonna and wanna are short forms. This listening uses the full forms.
