This letter is practice. It is not insurance advice.

A. Read the letter from Northline Cover.

Dear Hector,

We received your claim form. This letter is about a cracked phone screen. Nobody was hurt. The form was received on Monday. The photo was attached. Thank you for sending it. Please keep a copy of the form at home. You do not need to send the same photo again.

Your policy number is four two eight. Your reference number is seven one. Please keep both numbers on every page you send. Waiting on hold is tiring, so you do not have to call if the estimate is complete. You can write to customer service instead. A short letter is enough.

We still need the estimate. Sending a photo helps. The estimate shows the cost to fix the screen. Please send the estimate as an attachment. Put the policy number on the first line. You have to include it. If the number is missing, we cannot match the file to your claim. Write the reference number on the same line so the two numbers stay together.

The claim is in review. A resolution is not ready yet. Filing a claim takes time. A file like this often takes about two weeks after the estimate arrives. That time is only for this practice letter. It is not a promise. Please do not call every day while you wait.

If you want a person to look, write: I was wondering if you could check the claim. You can also write: Would you mind looking up the reference number? Please use statement order after if: if you could, not if could you. A polite sentence is easier to answer than a complaint with no facts.

A dry water stain is a different kind of claim. This file is only the cracked screen. Do not add a stain to this letter. The home in this practice is safe. The water-stain card in class is already dry. Leave it out of this file. Do not describe a bigger problem than the screen.

Customer service is open from nine to five on weekdays. If you call, have the reference number ready. You can also reply by letter. Paragraph 1 should say what happened and what was sent. Paragraph 2 should say what you are asking, with I was wondering if, and a thank-you close. Sign your name under the thank-you.

Sincerely, Ms. Lane Customer service Northline Cover

lessons.teacher:
Lesson 11 (Week 12): I'd Like to File a Claim

At a glance

Objectives: learners can…

  • start a sentence with a gerund (Waiting on hold is tiring)
  • soften a request with I was wondering if…
  • say what was sent or attached, in the passive
  • write a 1–2 paragraph letter

Today you will: Start with a gerund. • Soften a request. • Write a short letter.

By the end of class, you can do these four things. Every goal is a good goal.

  • I can start a sentence with a gerund (Waiting on hold is tiring).
  • I can soften a request with I was wondering if….
  • I can say what was sent or attached, in the passive.
  • I can write a 1–2 paragraph letter.

Materials

  • Student pages for Lesson 11
  • Claim cards: cracked screen; a dry water stain on a page
  • Status cards: received, missing the photo, in review
  • Listening: L5_L11_listening.mp3 (2:02). No speaker? Read the script aloud with a volunteer.
  • Prep time: 15 minutes

Key vocabulary

★ claim form • ★ policy number • ★ photo • ★ estimate • ★ complaint • ★ attachment • ★ reference number • ★ customer service • ★ on hold • ★ resolution • cracked screen • water stain

Clock-time plan

TimeStepMinGrouping (15 / 7–8)If running behind
6:00–6:06Opening Talk + Homework Check6PairsOne card only
6:06–6:12New Words + pair game6Whole class, then pairs★ words only
6:12–6:32Listening + Hear it, say it20Individuals, then pairsTask C on the board
6:32–6:45Grammar Q&A + pair check13Whole class, then pairsSkip the pair check
6:45–7:00BREAK15
7:00–7:18Talk Time: The Call + Letter Outline18PairsRound 1 only
7:18–7:25Read & Write7Pairs read, then writingQuestions only
7:25–7:30Exit Ticket + Homework5IndividualsNever skip

15: pairs, then switch roles with a new card. 7–8: pairs. 5 or fewer: one call the group coaches, then individual outlines.

Step by step

Step 1 · 6:00–6:06 · Opening Talk + Homework Check · 6 min

  • Opening Talk: A asks a card question. B answers in about four sentences. A asks one follow-up. Then switch.
  • Homework Check: pairs read one so… that or such… that sentence from Lesson 10. Write 2 corrections on the board. No names.
  • If behind: one card only.

Step 2 · 6:06–6:12 · New Words · 6 min

  • Point, say, repeat. ★ = most important.
  • Show: a claim form is the paper. A policy number and a reference number are two different numbers. An attachment is a file you send with a letter. On hold means you are waiting on the phone. A resolution is the answer at the end. The cracked screen is the phone. The water stain is already dry.
  • Check the meaning: "Is Waiting one activity or many?" (One.) • "Does the verb after Waiting take is or are?" (is) • "Was the photo attached, or did Hector forget it?" (It was attached.)
  • Partner game: A points. B makes a sentence. 15: 3 teams. 7–8: 2 teams. 5 or fewer: one team against the clock.

Step 3 · 6:12–6:32 · Listening + Hear it, say it · 20 min

  • Before you listen: Hector calls about a cracked-screen claim. Ms. Lane says the form was received and asks him to send the estimate.
  • Voices: Narrator, Hector, and Ms. Lane.
  • Play 1 → Task A. Play 2 → Tasks B and C.
  • Hear it, say it: gonna and wanna are short forms. This listening uses the full forms. You can say going to and want to. Say I was wondering if as one soft chunk. Keep the -ing in filing, waiting, and sending.
  • This letter is practice. It is not insurance advice.

Step 4 · 6:32–6:45 · Grammar Q&A + pair check · 13 min

  • Box 1: the -ing word is the subject. Waiting on hold is tiring. Filing a claim takes time. Sending a photo helps.
  • Box 2: I was wondering if you could check the claim. Statement order after if. Would you mind looking up the reference number?
  • Box 3: The photo was attached. The form was received.
  • Box 4: You have to include the policy number. You don't have to stay on hold.
  • Rule of thumb: A gerund subject is one activity, treated as it. The verb after it is singular: Waiting is, not Waiting are.
  • Pair check: A reads a gerund subject. B finishes with a singular verb. Then switch.
  • Break: On the board: Waiting is… / I was wondering if you could… / was attached.

Step 5 · 7:00–7:18 · Talk Time · 18 min

  • Round 1, The Call: A is the customer with a claim card (cracked screen, or a dry water stain). B is customer service with a status card (received, missing the photo, or in review). A must use I was wondering if and one gerund subject. Then switch.
  • Round 2, Letter Outline: pairs list the two paragraphs (what happened; what you are asking) before anyone writes full sentences.
  • 15: pairs, then switch with a new card. 7–8: pairs. 5 or fewer: one call the group coaches, then individual outlines.
  • Do not ask if learners have filed a claim. Invented facts only.

Step 6 · 7:18–7:25 · Read & Write · 7 min

  • Read the claim-status letter. Pairs answer the five questions.
  • Write a two-paragraph reply, about 8–12 sentences. Paragraph 1: what happened and what was sent. Paragraph 2: what you are asking, with I was wondering if and a thank-you. Start in class. Finish at home. Bring it next week.
  • This letter is practice. It is not insurance advice.

Step 7 · 7:25–7:30 · Exit Ticket + Homework · 5 min · NEVER SKIP

  • Exit ticket: Start a claim letter. Four sentences: a gerund subject, one passive, the request, and a polite close.
  • Homework: do item 1 together. Waiting on hold ____ tiring. → is. About 20–25 minutes. Bring the finished letter next week.

Listening script

2:02. The phone call is the whole story. Spoken lines use going to and want to.

Narrator: Lesson eleven. Hector calls customer service about a cracked phone screen. Ms. Lane answers. The phone call is the whole story.

Ms. Lane: Thank you for calling customer service. This is Ms. Lane. How can I help you?

Hector: Hello. I want to file a claim for a cracked screen. Waiting on hold was tiring, but I'm glad you answered.

Ms. Lane: I can help. What is your policy number?

Hector: It is four two eight. I was wondering if you could look up my claim.

Ms. Lane: The form was received. The claim is about a cracked screen. Is that right?

Hector: Yes. Filing a claim takes time, so I sent a photo last week.

Ms. Lane: The photo was attached. Sending a photo helps, but we still need the estimate.

Hector: I was wondering if you could tell me the reference number. I want to send the estimate today.

Ms. Lane: The reference number is seven one. Please send the estimate as an attachment.

Hector: Would you mind saying that number again? I want to write it on the claim form.

Ms. Lane: Of course. Seven one. You have to include the policy number on the estimate.

Hector: Sending the estimate is my next step. I don't want to stay on hold again.

Ms. Lane: You don't have to wait on hold. You can send the attachment with the reference number.

Hector: This is not a water stain. A water stain can be a claim too, but that stain is already dry. Nobody was hurt.

Ms. Lane: This file is only the cracked screen. The home is safe. When the estimate arrives, we can look for a resolution.

Hector: I'm going to send it today. Thank you for your help.

Ms. Lane: Thank you, Hector. A clear photo and a clear estimate are enough for this practice file.

Narrator: That's the end of the listening.

Answer key

  • Listening Task A: b (A cracked phone screen.)
  • Listening Task B: 1 was received, 2 was attached, 3 the estimate, 4 seven one, 5 four two eight, 6 send it today.
  • Listening Task C: 1 Waiting, 2 was received, 3 was attached, 4 Filing, 5 Sending, 6 Sending.
  • Grammar Practice A: 1 is, 2 attached, 3 takes, 4 could, 5 received, 6 helps.
  • Grammar Practice B: 1 is, 2 you could, 3 attached, 4 Filing, 5 have to, 6 helps.
  • Homework 1: is.
  • Read & Write: 1 A cracked phone screen. 2 The photo. 3 The estimate. 4 Seven one. 5 Four two eight.
  • Exit ticket: four sentences: a gerund subject, one passive, the request, and a polite close.

Teacher notes

  • This letter is practice. It is not insurance advice. For a real claim, use the phone number on your own policy.
  • The damage is a phone screen or a dry stain. Nobody is hurt, and the home is safe. Do not invent a fire, a flood, or an injury.
  • Do not ask if learners have filed a claim.
  • I was wondering if could you is the wrong order. Say if you could.
  • gonna and wanna are short forms. This listening uses the full forms.

A short library meeting. Ms. Adeyemi chairs. Tom wants later hours. Grace wants the current hours, because the bus she takes stops early. They agree to a one-month try.

Voices: Ms. Adeyemi, Tom, and Grace. A narrator opens and closes the listening.

A. Listen. What are they deciding? Circle.

a. A new library building. b. Evening hours. c. The price of a bus pass.

B. Listen again. Circle the answers.

  1. Tom wants: (later hours / the current hours / a new bus)
  2. Grace wants: (later hours / the current hours / no meeting)
  3. Grace's reason: (the bus stops early / the room is cold / she wants a microphone)

sections.title: Grammar
sections.html:
Grammar Box 1: which for a thing

WHICH + THINGNO EXTRA IT
The proposal which the chair readis on page 2.
The library which we usecloses at six.
The agenda which is on the handoutlists the hours.

Grammar Box 2: where for a place

WHERE REPLACES THEREEXAMPLE
This is the room where we meet.Not: the room which we meet.
The stop where I catch the busis dark after seven.
The place where we should meetis this library room.

Grammar Box 3: who for a person

WHO, NOT WHICHEXAMPLE
The person who takes notesis the secretary.
The chairperson who keeps the orderis Ms. Adeyemi.
The person who rides the busis Grace.

Grammar Box 4: an opinion and a reason

YOU CAN SAYEXAMPLE
I think…I think a one-month try is fair.
I see your point, but…I see your point, but I need a safe ride.
Which or whereWhich idea? Where would you say it?

Rule of thumb: Which and who tell you which thing or person. Do not add it or he after them (the proposal which the chair read, not which the chair read it). Where replaces there.

Questions and answers

Q: The room which we meet. Right or wrong?

A: Wrong. The room where we meet.

Q: Can I say the proposal which the chair read it?

A: No. Drop it.

Q: The person which takes notes. Right or wrong?

  2. The proposal (which / where) the chair read is on page 2.

Don't saySay

sections.title: Read & Write
sections.html:
A. Read the agenda and the proposal.

River Bend Library · Evening hours meeting

Agenda

  1. Welcome and the sign-in sheet
  2. The proposal, which is on page 2 of this handout
  3. Questions, one question card each
  4. A decision

Please sign in before you sit down. Write your name the same way it appears on your name tent. If you arrive late, add your name at the bottom. The minutes will list the people who signed in. Please wear a name tent. The chairperson is Ms. Adeyemi. The person who takes notes will write the minutes. Use the microphone when you speak. The timer is four minutes for each speaker. We are in the room where we meet. We are not in the auditorium. The auditorium is too big for this group.

Proposal: a one-month try of later hours

The library which we use now closes at six. Some workers cannot come before six. Tom's proposal says the library stays open until eight on Thursday for one month. The handout shows the same idea. He thinks a short try is fair. He is going to come after work if the hours change. He does not want the library open late every night. Thursday is the only day in the proposal.

Grace does not want the change every night. The bus she takes stops early. The stop where she catches the bus is dark after seven. She can agree to Thursday only, if the sign-in sheet shows how many people come. She wants a safe ride home. That is her reason. She sees Tom's point, but she will not give up the bus.

The chair asks each person for one reason. A useful sentence is: I think a one-month try is fair. Another is: I see your point, but I need a safe ride. The decision is about hours. It is not an election, and it is not about a party. At the end, the chair reads one sentence: the decision and one reason. Example: We will try Thursday hours until eight for one month, because workers need a later time and riders need a safe bus.

If your group prefers a school conference, use the same English. The question can be: Which time works, and where will we meet? A parent or a volunteer can both use the card. Do not talk about grades. Do not talk about discipline. The chair still keeps the order and still stops at four minutes.

Lesson 12 (Week 13): The Room Where We Meet

Objectives: learners can…

Narrator: Lesson twelve. This is a short meeting at the library. Ms. Adeyemi is the chairperson. Tom and Grace are going to talk about evening hours.

Tom: I want to speak about the proposal. I want later hours.

Grace: I see your point, but I want to keep the current hours. The bus I take stops early.

Tom: The library which we use closes at six. I want it open until eight.

Grace: The stop where I catch the bus is dark after seven. That is my reason.

Ms. Adeyemi: The person who takes notes is writing the minutes. Please use the microphone when you speak.

Tom: I think a one-month try is fair. I'm going to come after work on Thursday.

Tom: I want to ask one question. Which bus still runs at eight?

sections.title: Grammar
sections.html:
This is a talk frame, not a new tense.

Grammar Box 1: introduction

THE INTRODUCTIONIT NAMES THE POINT
I've been learning to speak up at work.That is my point.
A mentor helped me.That is part of the point.
I want to give two examples.Then the examples start.

Grammar Box 2: two examples

THE EXAMPLEA DETAIL
Example 1By the time I finished my first month, I had learned to pause.
The hard momentI wish I had looked up sooner, so next time I will make eye contact.
Example 2My mentor asked one question.

Grammar Box 3: conclusion

THE CONCLUSIONNOT A NEW STORY
Repeat the point in new words.I can speak from notes.
Add a next step.I'm going to practice one talk a week.
Stop.Applause is for finishing.

Grammar Box 4: review sentences, not a new tense

REVIEWONE SENTENCE
I've been learning…I've been learning to speak up at work.
By the time I finished…, I had…By the time I finished my first month, I had learned to pause.
I wish I had…, so next time I will…I wish I had looked up sooner, so next time I will make eye contact.
I'm going to…I'm going to practice with a stopwatch.

Rule of thumb: The introduction names the point. Each example has a detail. The conclusion repeats the point in new words and adds a next step.

Questions and answers

Q: Can the talk start with the example?

A: No. The introduction names the point first.

Q: Can the conclusion be a new story?

A: No. It repeats the point and adds a next step.

Q: Can I say I gonna practice?

A: No. Say I'm going to practice.

  3. My mentor asked one question. ____________

  6. I wish I had looked up sooner, so next time I will make eye contact. ____________

Practice B: Circle the correct words.

  1. The introduction (names the point / tells a new story).
  2. Each example (has a detail / has no detail).
  3. The conclusion (is a new story / repeats the point).
  4. Next step: (I'm going to / I gonna) practice.
  5. By the time I finished, I (had learned / have learn) to pause.
  6. I've been (learning / learn) to speak up.

Common mistakes

Don't saySay
Start with the example and never say the point.Start with the introduction. It names the point.
A conclusion that is a new story.The conclusion repeats the point and adds a next step.
I gonna practice.I'm going to practice.

1:47. Spoken lines use going to and want to.
